body.text: SR&ED supporting documentation is the contemporaneous, dated evidence Canadian businesses keep to substantiate Scientific Research and Experimental Development claims under the federal Income Tax Act. CRA reviewers examine test records, photographs, ledgers, receipts, contracts and equipment usage logs, so claimants must generate this evidence as work progresses to support eligibility and expenditures.

Canada’s flagship innovation tax incentive, the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program, is jointly governed by the Department of Finance Canada—which establishes the legislative framework under the federal Income Tax Act (ITA) and Income Tax Regulations (ITR)—and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), which administers technical and financial compliance across all provinces and territories1. Under the federal regime, claimants access two distinct, sequential incentives: first, taxpayers carrying on business in Canada may pool and deduct qualifying SR&ED expenditures against business income in the current taxation year or carry them forward indefinitely under Section 37 of the ITA5; second, claimants earn volume-based Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) under Section 127 and Section 127.1 of the ITA ranging from a basic rate of 15% to an enhanced rate of 35% on qualified SR&ED expenditures, with unused credits eligible for a 3-year carryback and a 20-year carryforward1.

Following the enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, Canada implemented the most expansive structural modernization of the SR&ED regime in over a decade, effective retroactively for taxation years beginning after December 15, 20241. Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3 million to $6 million, widened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, introduced an elective 3-year average revenue phase-out alternative for Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs), extended the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restored the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures, shared-use equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 20241. Concurrently, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval process allowing eligible businesses with under $25 million in gross business income to obtain upfront technical eligibility determinations within an eight-week service standard before incurring project costs7.

At the provincial and territorial level, corporate claimants can stack regional R&D tax credits on top of federal incentives, though provincial credits constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(18) of the ITA and therefore reduce the federal Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and Section 127 qualified expenditure base12. Notably, Québec enacted a sweeping overhaul in its March 25, 2025 budget (effective for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025), eliminating eight legacy provincial R&D tax measures and replacing them with the fully refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), which provides a 30% credit on the first $1 million of qualified R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures (including capital equipment) above an exclusion threshold and 20% on excess spending15. In Ontario, the three-tier structure—comprising the 8% refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC, capped at a $3 million expenditure limit), the 20% refundable Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC, capped at $20 million), and the 3.5% non-refundable Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC)—remains in force without mirroring the federal $6 million limit increase13.
1. Statutory and Legislative Framework of the Federal SR&ED Program
1.1 Dual-Mechanism Architecture Under the Income Tax Act

The federal SR&ED tax incentive regime has operated in its modern statutory structure since 1985 and is codified across three primary pillars of the Income Tax Act and the Income Tax Regulations2. Unlike jurisdictions that rely solely on super-deductions or standalone tax credits, the Canadian federal system delivers two distinct, sequential tax incentives that must be calculated separately in tax working papers3.

First, under Section 37 of the ITA (Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures), a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada in a taxation year may deduct qualifying current expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(a)) and—for property acquired after December 15, 2024—qualifying capital expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(b)) incurred on SR&ED carried on in Canada directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer and related to a business of the taxpayer5. Under subsection 37(1.1), if a corporate taxpayer performs SR&ED related to a business actively carried on by a related corporation at the time of the expenditure, the SR&ED is deemed related to a business of the taxpayer5. Rather than depreciating R&D costs over multiple years or amortizing them, taxpayers aggregate allowable expenditures into a running pool6. The positive balance of this pool may be deducted in full or in part in the current taxation year to reduce net income for tax purposes, or carried forward indefinitely to offset business income in any subsequent taxation year5. For current expenditures on SR&ED carried on outside Canada directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer (or payments to approved foreign institutions/universities where the taxpayer is entitled to exploit the results), subsection 37(2) permits a current-year deduction from business income, although such foreign expenditures (save for limited permissible Canadian-resident employee wages under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5)) cannot enter the subsection 37(1) pool or earn an ITC5.

Second, under Section 127 and Section 127.1 of the ITA (SR&ED Investment Tax Credit), taxpayers earn an Investment Tax Credit under subsection 127(5) and the definitions in subsection 127(9), calculated as a percentage of their "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" at the end of the taxation year8. Subsection 127(10.1) provides the statutory authority for the enhanced ITC (an additional 20% credit atop the 15% basic credit, yielding 35%) for qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs up to their annual expenditure limit8. Section 127.1 governs the refundability of unused ITCs, defining "refundable investment tax credit" under subsection 127.1(2) and providing supplementary refundability rules for non-qualifying CCPCs under subsection 127.1(2.01)8.

Third, under Regulation 2900, Regulation 2902, Regulation 2903, and Regulation 4600 of the Income Tax Regulations, the operational mechanics of expenditure eligibility are defined by regulation19. Regulation 2900 governs expenditures directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED under the traditional method (subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3)), the calculation of the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under the proxy method (subsection 2900(4)), and the definition of Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) excluded from shared-use equipment treatment (subsection 2900(11))10. Regulation 2902 enumerates "prescribed expenditures" that are statutorily barred from entering the qualified expenditure base for ITC purposes19. Consequential to the post-December 15, 2024 restoration of capital expenditures, paragraph 2902(b) was amended to allow eligible capital and shared-use equipment into the ITC base, while new Regulation 2903 specifies what constitutes a prescribed special-purpose building20. Subsections 4600(1) and 4600(2) of the Regulations further set out rules referenced in investment tax credit calculations22.

A foundational principle of Canadian R&D tax auditing is that "allowable SR&ED expenditures" (deductible under Section 37) and "qualified SR&ED expenditures" (eligible for ITCs under Section 127) are not interchangeable terms7. An expenditure may be 100% deductible under Section 37 while only 80% eligible for an ITC (such as arm's-length Canadian subcontractor payments and third-party payments), or 0% eligible for an ITC (such as non-arm's-length contract payments without a Form T1146 transfer, or the acquisition of used capital equipment)19. Conversely, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) generates an ITC under Section 127 but is a notional figure that can never be deducted under Section 3719.
1.2 Statutory Definition of SR&ED Under Subsection 248(1)

The legal definition of "scientific research and experimental development" is housed in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act and generally conforms to the international standards of the OECD Frascati Manual1. Under subsection 248(1), SR&ED means a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and that falls within one of three core categories of research—basic research, applied research, or experimental development—or one category of eligible support work, while expressly excluding seven enumerated commercial or routine activities1.

In the core research categories, paragraph 248(1)(a) (Basic Research) covers work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view3. Basic research expands the existing scientific knowledge base, is traditionally performed by universities, government laboratories, non-profit institutions, and modern biotechnology or advanced technology firms, and typically yields results published in scientific journals3. Paragraph 248(1)(b) (Applied Research) covers work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view3. Because both applied research and experimental development are conducted with a practical application in view, CRA administrative guidelines note that many operational characteristics of experimental development extend directly to applied research3. Paragraph 248(1)(c) (Experimental Development)—which represents the most commonly claimed category of SR&ED work in Canada—covers work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto3. The statutory inclusion of "incremental improvements thereto" confirms that revolutionary breakthroughs are not required; gradual, step-by-step advances in technology qualify provided they seek to resolve genuine technological uncertainty3.

Under paragraph 248(1)(d) (Support Work), SR&ED includes work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight exhaustive statutory categories: (1) engineering, (2) design, (3) operations research, (4) mathematical analysis, (5) computer programming, (6) data collection, (7) testing, or (8) psychological research, where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer3. Support work is never SR&ED on its own; its eligibility is strictly derivative of, and proportionate to, underlying basic research, applied research, or experimental development conducted in Canada3.
To establish clear statutory boundaries between R&D and commercial operations, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) explicitly exclude seven categories of work from the definition of SR&ED3:

items: Paragraph (e): Market research or sales promotion3;
Paragraph (f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes3;
Paragraph (g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities3;
Paragraph (h): Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas3;
Paragraph (i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process3;
Paragraph (j): Style changes3; and
Paragraph (k): Routine data collection3.

body.text: 1.3 The CRA Eligibility Framework: The "Why" and "How" Requirements

On August 13, 2021, the CRA published its consolidated Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives, replacing the legacy Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy3. The CRA guidelines synthesize the statutory language of subsection 248(1) and common law jurisprudence into two mandatory requirements—the "Why" requirement and the "How" requirement—both of which must be met for work to be eligible as SR&ED3.
The "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Advancement and Uncertainty)

The "Why" requirement examines the underlying purpose of the work: it must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement3. The CRA distinguishes between conceptual knowledge (theories, principles, or prediction models explaining why or how a system behaves) and merely factual knowledge (isolated data or measurements)3. Eligible SR&ED focuses on generating or discovering conceptual knowledge, though categorizing that knowledge as strictly "scientific" versus "technological" is not critical because both qualify3.

New scientific or technological knowledge is required only when it is unknown or uncertain whether a given result or objective can be achieved—or how to achieve it—due to an insufficiency in the available scientific or technological knowledge base3. The CRA defines the "scientific or technological knowledge base" as the combined scientific and technological knowledge of the resources within the claimant's business alongside all sources that are reasonably available publicly3. Recognizing scientific or technological uncertainty marks the starting point of SR&ED work, and attempting to resolve this uncertainty constitutes an attempt to achieve scientific or technological advancement3.
In the context of experimental development, the CRA guidelines identify eight characteristics of technical problems that suggest existing technological knowledge is insufficient3:

items: Existing design methods are not applicable3;
Requirements or specifications do not conform to existing standards3;
Too many variables or unknowns exist3;
Parameters or conditions are outside the normal operating range3;
The nature of the problem is evolving3;
Data is not readily available3;
Interlocking constraints exist3; or
Economic considerations or cost targets impose a technological uncertainty3.

body.text: Critically, acquiring available knowledge or know-how that already exists—such as through training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or consultants, or purchasing proprietary knowledge—does not meet the requirement of attempting to achieve technological advancement3. Similarly, if an uncertainty is circumvented using available knowledge or a workaround without attempting to resolve the underlying uncertainty, the work is not eligible3. Conversely, success or failure in meeting project objectives does not affect eligibility under the "Why" requirement; the statutory definition requires only that the purpose of the work be to achieve scientific or technological advancement3.
The "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search)

The "How" requirement governs the methodology of the work: it is not sufficient for work to merely follow a systematic business practice or standard procedure3. The approach must be a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology carried out by means of experiment or analysis, encompassing four key operational elements3:

items: Generating an Idea or Hypothesis: Formulating an idea consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for further investigation toward achieving the objective or resolving the problem (expressed as a possible solution, proposed method, or approach)3;
Testing by Experiment or Analysis: Testing the idea or hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis, where the idea can evolve and change as a result of testing3;
Developing Logical Conclusions: Developing logical conclusions based on the results or findings of the experiment or analysis3; and
Keeping Contemporaneous Evidence: Keeping evidence that is generated as the work progresses3.

body.text: Distinguishing Support Work from Excluded Work

Because activities such as testing and data collection appear in both paragraph 248(1)(d) (eligible support work) and paragraphs 248(1)(f) and (k) (excluded routine testing and routine data collection), the CRA evaluates purpose as the key feature distinguishing the two3. If data collection or testing is carried out specifically to directly support scientific research or experimental development in Canada, it qualifies as eligible support work under paragraph 248(1)(d)3. If the work is conducted for some other reason—such as supporting normal business operations, routine quality control, or routine commercial data collection—it is excluded3. Likewise, where a business conducts eligible SR&ED while simultaneously prospecting for minerals, the eligible SR&ED work may be claimed, but the mineral prospecting work must be carved out and excluded under paragraph 248(1)(h)3.
1.4 Landmark 2024–2026 Legislative Reforms: Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1)

Between late 2024 and early 2026, the federal SR&ED program underwent a multi-stage legislative expansion designed to reverse the 2012–2014 base reductions and boost domestic R&D investment1. Practitioners auditing claims across the 2024, 2025, and 2026 taxation years must track the precise legislative evolution from initial proposal to enacted law:

In the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES) and August 2025 Draft Legislation, the Department of Finance initially proposed increasing the expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3 million to $4.5 million (as reflected in the August 2025 draft explanatory notes to subsection 127(10.6)), widening the taxable capital phase-out thresholds to $15 million–$75 million, extending the enhanced 35% ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restoring the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 20248. Subsequently, in Budget 2025 (Canada Strong), the federal government further increased the enhanced expenditure limit ceiling to $6 million (investing $930 million to expand the SR&ED program)1. These measures were enacted into law via Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 20261. All core rate, threshold, and ECPC amendments apply retroactively to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (i.e., on or after December 16, 2024), while the restored capital expenditure, shared-use equipment, and lease cost rules apply to property acquired and lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 20248.

Consequential to restoring capital expenditure eligibility under paragraph 37(1)(b), Bill C-15 repealed subsections 37(14) and 37(15) of the ITA (the contract "look-through rule") for property acquired and lease costs first payable on or after December 16, 202420. Between 2014 and December 15, 2024, when capital expenditures were ineligible, subsection 37(14) required a payer's SR&ED contract expenditure to be reduced by any related non-current (capital) expenditure of the contractor/performer, and subsection 37(15) required the performer to notify the payer in writing of the reduction amount without delay upon request and no later than 90 days after the end of the calendar year20. With capital expenditures restored after December 15, 2024, contract expenditures and third-party payments are no longer reduced by the performer's non-current expenditures20.

Additionally, on June 20, 2024, Bill C-69 amended the definition of "government assistance" in subsection 127(9) of the ITA to specify that excluded loans (as defined in subsection 12(11)) bearing reasonable repayment terms are not treated as government assistance, effective retroactively to January 1, 2020 (for loans made after December 31, 2019), allowing claimants who previously deducted such loans on Form T661 to amend returns for taxation years that are not statute-barred9.

body.text: 2. Federal Investment Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, Refundability, and Pool Mechanics
2.1 Basic (15%) and Enhanced (35%) Investment Tax Credit Rates

Canada’s federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit is a purely volume-based corporate or personal income tax offset—meaning the credit rate applies to the total dollar volume of qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in the taxation year, with a 0% incremental rate component1. Under subsections 127(5), 127(9), and 127(10.1) of the ITA, two statutory credit rates apply8.

The Basic ITC Rate of 15% (reduced from 20% after 2013) applies generally to a claimant's SR&ED qualified expenditure pool8. This 15% rate is earned by all corporations other than qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs (such as foreign-controlled subsidiaries and large public corporations exceeding the revenue phase-out threshold), sole proprietorships (individuals), partners of a partnership, and beneficiaries of trusts, as well as on qualified expenditures incurred by CCPCs and ECPCs in excess of their annual expenditure limit8.

The Enhanced ITC Rate of 35% (consisting of the 15% basic rate plus a 20% addition under subsection 127(10.1) of the ITA) is earned by qualifying CCPCs and—for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024—qualifying ECPCs on their qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual expenditure limit ($6 million for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024; $3 million for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024)8.
2.2 Entity Qualification: CCPC and ECPC Statutory Rules
Access to the 35% enhanced rate and cash refundability depends on corporate status definitions in subsection 125(7) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA1.
Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC) Requirements
A corporation qualifies as a CCPC under subsection 125(7) of the ITA if it meets all eight of the following conditions at the end of the taxation year1:

items: It is a private corporation1;
It is a corporation resident in Canada and was either incorporated in Canada or resident in Canada from June 18, 1971, to the end of the taxation year1;
It is not controlled directly or indirectly by one or more non-resident persons1;
It is not controlled directly or indirectly by one or more public corporations (other than a prescribed venture capital corporation under Regulation 6700 of the Income Tax Regulations)1;
It is not controlled by a Canadian-resident corporation that lists its shares on a designated stock exchange outside of Canada1;
It is not controlled directly or indirectly by any combination of persons described above1;

If all of its shares that are owned by a non-resident person, by a public corporation (other than a prescribed venture capital corporation), or by a corporation with a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange outside Canada were owned by one single hypothetical person, that person would not own sufficient shares to control the corporation1; and
No class of its capital stock is listed on a designated stock exchange1.

body.text: Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) Requirements

Defined in subsection 127(9) of the ITA and applicable to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, an ECPC is defined generally as a corporation that meets the following criteria throughout the taxation year1:

items: It is resident in Canada1;
It is a "public corporation" as defined in the ITA (or would be a public corporation if the phrase "designated stock exchange in Canada" in that definition were read as "designated stock exchange")1;
It is not controlled by one or more non-resident persons1;
It would not be controlled by a particular non-resident person if all shares of the corporation owned by non-resident persons were owned by that single hypothetical person1; or
It is an eligible subsidiary of a corporation that satisfies the conditions above1.

body.text: Partnerships, Trusts, and Sole Proprietorships

In computing the income of a partnership under subsection 96(1) and paragraph 96(1)(e.1) of the ITA (and subsection 1102(1a) of the Regulations for partnership property), SR&ED expenditures and property are accounted for at the partnership level6. Because a partnership cannot carry forward a pool balance of deductible SR&ED expenditures to a subsequent fiscal period, the Section 37 pool balance must be fully deducted in calculating partnership net income in the year incurred6. The resulting ITC is allocated to the members of the partnership under subsection 127(8) at the basic 15% rate8. Sole proprietorships (individuals) and beneficiaries of trusts also earn ITCs at the basic 15% rate29.
2.3 Expenditure Limits and Phase-Out Formulas

Subsections 127(10.2) through 127(10.64) of the ITA establish the annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced ITC and phase that limit out as a corporation (together with its associated CCPCs or consolidated ECPCs) exceeds statutory capital or revenue thresholds8.
1. Legacy Formula for CCPCs (Taxation Years Beginning Before December 16, 2024)

For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the maximum expenditure limit is $3,000,000 (for CCPCs only) and decreases based on the taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC (and all associated CCPCs) for the previous taxation year8. The reduction begins once prior-year taxable capital reaches $10,000,000 and becomes nil at $50,000,0008.
2. Enacted Bill C-15 Formula for CCPCs – Taxable Capital Method (Taxation Years Beginning After December 15, 2024)

Under amended subsection 127(10.2) of the ITA, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the baseline expenditure limit is $6,000,000 and phases out linearly where the CCPC’s (or associated CCPC group's) prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is between $15,000,000 and $75,000,0001:

In this statutory formula, A is nil ($0) if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is $15,000,000 or less, or equals the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000, reducing the expenditure limit to nil once prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,0001.
3. Enacted Bill C-15 Formula for ECPCs and Electing CCPCs – Revenue Method (Taxation Years Beginning After December 15, 2024)

Under subsection 127(10.6) of the ITA, an ECPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit is phased out based on the corporation's (or consolidated ECPC group's, under subsections 127(10.61) to 127(10.63) and the definition of "consolidated financial statements" in subsection 233.8(1)) average annual revenue over the three preceding fiscal years between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, becoming nil at $75,000,000 or greater1. Furthermore, under new subsections 127(10.31) (for a single CCPC) and 127(10.32) (for a CCPC having associated corporations), a CCPC or associated CCPC group may elect on a prescribed form to have its $6,000,000 expenditure limit determined using this same 3-year average annual revenue method ($15,000,000 to $75,000,000 phase-out) instead of the subsection 127(10.2) taxable capital method1.
Associated Corporations, Consolidated Groups, and Short Taxation Years

Associated CCPCs must share the group expenditure limit under subsections 127(10.21) and 127(10.3) by filing an allocation agreement on Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit) (updated May 29, 2026)8. If associated corporations fail to file an agreement, subsection 127(10.4) authorizes the Minister to allocate the limit8, while subsections 127(10.22) and 127(10.23) govern deemed non-association of corporations8. Similarly, consolidated ECPCs share a single expenditure limit under subsections 127(10.61) and 127(10.62)8, and paragraph 87(2)(j.6) provides continuity rules on corporate amalgamations20.

Under subsection 127(10.5) (renumbered from former subsection 127(10.6)) and subsection 127(10.64), the expenditure limit is prorated for short taxation years or when a CCPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year while associated with another CCPC8. For example, if Corporation P is allocated a $3,000,000 expenditure limit and has a 184-day short taxation year running from July 1 to December 31, 2027, its expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.5) is calculated as $3,000,000 × (184 days ÷ 365 days) = $1,512,3288.
2.4 Refundability Rules Under Section 127.1

Under Section 127.1 of the ITA, claimants can receive all or part of their current-year unused ITC balance (after offsetting Part I tax payable under subsection 127(5)) as a cash refund, depending on their entity classification and whether the expenditures are of a current or capital nature1.

2.5 Carryforward, Carryback, and Section 37 Deduction Pool Mechanics
Carryover of Unused Investment Tax Credits

Unused SR&ED ITCs that are not refunded or used to offset Part I tax in the current year may be carried back 3 years to reduce Part I tax in any of the three preceding taxation years or carried forward up to 20 taxation years to offset future Part I tax payable1. An acquisition of control restricts the carryforward of unused ITCs earned before the acquisition as well as the carryback of unused ITCs earned after the acquisition8.
Taxability of Used or Refunded Federal ITCs (One-Year Lag Rule)

Used and refunded federal SR&ED ITCs are included in taxable income in the following taxation year1. Specifically, under paragraph 37(1)(e) of the ITA, any federal SR&ED ITC deducted under subsection 127(5) or refunded in a preceding taxation year (including ITCs attributable to proxy amounts, current qualified expenditures, or pool additions under paragraph 127(13)(e)) reduces the balance of the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the subsequent taxation year5. If this reduction causes the Section 37 pool balance at the end of that taxation year to become negative, the negative balance must be included in computing business income for that year under paragraph 12(1)(v) of the ITA1.
Additions and Subtractions to the Section 37 Pool
Determined in Section C of Part 3 of Form T661 under subsection 37(1) of the ITA, the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures acts as a running account with an indefinite carryforward period6.

The increases (additions) to the Section 37 pool consist of: (1) current expenditures incurred on SR&ED carried on in Canada under paragraph 37(1)(a), including directly engaged salaries/wages, materials consumed or transformed, post-December 15, 2024 equipment lease costs, SR&ED contracts performed on the claimant's behalf, eligible third-party payments, and traditional-method overhead5; (2) capital expenditures made on SR&ED in Canada under paragraph 37(1)(b) for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, once the property is available for use under subsection 37(1.2)5; (3) repayments of government or non-government assistance under paragraph 37(1)(c) that previously reduced the pool5; (4) amounts included in income in prior years due to a negative pool balance under paragraph 12(1)(v), added back under paragraph 37(1)(c.1) to reset the opening balance to nil5; (5) amounts added to tax payable in preceding years due to ITC recapture under subsections 127(27), (29), or (34) (paragraph 37(1)(c.2)) or partnership ITC recapture excess amounts under subsection 127(30) (paragraph 37(1)(c.3))5; and (6) pool balances transferred upon an amalgamation or wind-up6.

The decreases (subtractions) from the Section 37 pool consist of: (1) government or non-government assistance (defined in subsection 127(9)) received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received by the filing-due date under paragraph 37(1)(d)5; (2) provincial super-allowance benefit amounts under paragraph 37(1)(d.1)5; (3) ITCs applied and/or refunded in preceding taxation years under paragraph 37(1)(e)5; (4) amounts deducted from the pool under subsection 37(1) in preceding taxation years (excluding deemed CCA under subsection 37(6)) under paragraph 37(1)(f)5; (5) insolvency deductions claimed under section 61.3 in preceding years under paragraph 37(1)(f.1)5; (6) twice the amount claimed under subparagraph 194(2)(a)(ii) for preceding years under paragraph 37(1)(g)5; and (7) amounts determined under subsection 37(6.1) following a loss restriction event under paragraph 37(1)(h)5.
Loss Restriction Events, Acquisition of Rights, and Charitable Gift Exclusions

When a corporation undergoes an acquisition of control (or a trust acquires a new majority-interest beneficiary), a "loss restriction event" occurs5. Under paragraph 37(1)(h) and subsection 37(6.1) of the ITA, the pool is reduced and pre-acquisition SR&ED pool balances may only be reinstated and deducted in subsequent years when the business to which the SR&ED expenditures related is continued for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and only to the extent of income from that same or a similar business6.

Furthermore, under subsection 37(4) of the ITA and paragraph 2902(c) of the Regulations (and confirmed in Halak v. Minister of National Revenue, 89 D.T.C. 531), no Section 37 deduction and no Section 127 ITC is permitted for any expenditure made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED5. This rule ensures that only one claimant (the performer) receives SR&ED tax incentives on the work and prevents taxpayers from claiming Canadian tax incentives on rights resulting from R&D performed outside Canada6. Finally, subsection 37(5) prohibits a double deduction by barring any deduction as a charitable gift under section 110.1 (corporations) or section 118.1 (individuals) for an expenditure deductible under Section 375.
3. Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures and Calculation Methodologies
3.1 Election Between the Traditional Method and the Proxy Method

For each taxation year, a claimant must select either the Traditional Method or the Proxy Method in Part 3, Section A of Form T661 to compute its SR&ED expenditures19. Under subsection 37(10) of the ITA, the election is made on a year-by-year basis when Form T661 is first filed for the taxation year and is irrevocable for that taxation year once filed (though the claimant may select a different method in future taxation years)7. If a claimant does not select a method on Form T661, the CRA automatically processes the claim using the traditional method19.

Under the Traditional Method (Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) of the ITA & Subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3) of the ITR), the claimant specifically identifies, tracks, and allocates all overhead and other expenditures that are either all or substantially all (ASA, 90% or more) attributable, or directly attributable (both directly related and incremental), to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada or the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for SR&ED19. These actual overhead expenditures are included in both the Section 37 deductible pool (on Line 360 of Form T661) and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool to earn ITCs19.

Under the Proxy Method (Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the ITA & Subsection 2900(4) of the ITR), the claimant does not specifically identify or track overhead expenditures on Form T661, deducting actual overhead costs instead as regular business expenses19. In place of actual overhead, the claimant calculates a notional substitute amount—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—equal to 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base (calculated in Part 5 of Form T661)19. The PPA is included in Section 127 qualified expenditures (Line 502 of Form T661) to earn ITCs, but cannot be included in the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures19.

body.text: Comparative Numerical Illustration (Acme Ltd. – Traditional vs. Proxy Method)

As illustrated in Section 6.10 of the CRA Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy, consider a CCPC (earning the 35% enhanced ITC rate) that incurs $100,000 in directly engaged SR&ED salaries, $15,000 in materials consumed, and $50,000 in eligible SR&ED overhead expenditures19:

items: Under the Traditional Method: Additions to the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool total $100,000 (salaries) + $15,000 (materials) + $50,000 (overhead) = $165,00019. Because the PPA is $0 under the traditional method, total qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes are also $165,000 (generating a 35% ITC of $57,750)19.

Under the Proxy Method: Additions to the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool total $100,000 (salaries) + $15,000 (materials) = $115,000 (while the $50,000 in actual overhead remains deductible as an ordinary business expense)19. For ITC purposes, the company adds the Prescribed Proxy Amount of $55,000 (55% of the $100,000 salary base) to the $115,000 of allowable expenditures, resulting in $170,000 of total qualified SR&ED expenditures (generating a 35% ITC of $59,500)19.

body.text: 3.2 Salary or Wages Policy and Specified Employee Restrictions

Per the CRA SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), "salary or wages" is defined in subsection 248(1) of the ITA as the income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Act, including all fees received for services not rendered in the course of the taxpayer's business, but excluding superannuation or pension benefits or retiring allowances44.
Eligible Inclusions and Exclusions in SR&ED Salary or Wages

Allowable SR&ED salary or wages include regular gross salaries and wages paid to or incurred for employees in the taxation year for SR&ED work; vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, tips, gratuities, honorariums, director's fees, management fees, and commissions; inducement payments and non-competition payments to employees; bonuses and remuneration based on profits (only for employees other than specified employees); permissible salary or wages for SR&ED work carried on outside Canada; and taxable benefits under section 6 of the Act (where the actual cost is a reasonable estimate, excludes GST/HST or PST input tax credits under subsection 248(16), and is not claimed as a general business expense)44.

Conversely, the following items are excluded from SR&ED salary or wages: dividends (which do not constitute employment income)7; stock option benefits (considered not to be an expenditure incurred)44; retiring allowances, including accumulated vacation and sick leave credits upon retirement (though potentially allowable as overhead under the traditional method, never under the proxy method)19; extended vacation or sick leave (during which the employee is not directly undertaking, supporting, supervising, or directly engaged in SR&ED)44; the employer's share of related benefits (which may be claimed only as overhead under the traditional method)44; and unpaid salary or wages remaining unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year44.
"Directly Engaged" Employees vs. Indirect Support

Under the proxy method (and for Lines 300 and 305 of Form T661), only salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED can be claimed1. The CRA defines "directly engaged" as hands-on work determined by the actual tasks performed rather than the employee's job title1. This includes hands-on experimentation, operating machines required for an experiment, feeding raw materials into a machine under the supervision of staff with scientific or technological qualifications, and technological planning for ongoing claimed SR&ED projects (such as assigning technological personnel, setting job priorities, developing technological strategies, or evaluating quality of materials used)42. Where an employee's time spent directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada is all or substantially all (ASA, 90% or more) of their employment time, clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) deems the entire expenditure to be for SR&ED19. Under the traditional method, salaries of employees who directly undertake, supervise, or support SR&ED in tasks not considered "directly engaged" (such as long-term planning for future SR&ED projects or contract administration directly related to SR&ED), as well as clerical and administrative staff providing a direct and incremental service to SR&ED employees, can be claimed as overhead on Line 360 of Form T66119.
Unpaid Remuneration (The 180-Day Rule – Subsection 78(4))

Under subsection 78(4) of the ITA, if employee remuneration incurred in a taxation year remains unpaid 180 days after the end of that taxation year, the expenditure is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year, and is instead deemed to be incurred in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid44. A payment made on the 180th day is considered paid within the allowable time limit44. Reasonable vacation or holiday pay and deferred amounts payable under a salary deferral arrangement (as defined in subsection 248(1)) are exceptions deemed paid on the 180th day for Section 37 deductibility, though they are excluded from the salary base used to determine the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)26.
Rules for "Specified Employees" (Owner-Managers and Non-Arm's Length Staff)

A specified employee is defined in subsection 248(1) of the ITA and includes individuals who do not deal at arm's length with the employer or who are specified shareholders (such as a sole shareholder or significant owner-manager, or someone related to them)7. Three strict statutory limitations govern specified employees:

items: Exclusion of Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration (Subsection 37(9)): Under subsection 37(9) of the ITA, an expenditure on or in respect of SR&ED does not include a bonus or remuneration based on profits in respect of a person who is a specified employee of the payer7.

Maximum Allowable SR&ED Salary Cap (5 × YMPE): The maximum salary or wages claimable for a specified employee as an SR&ED expenditure (on Line 305 of Form T661) is limited to 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) as determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated for the number of days the individual was a specified employee during the taxation year43:

body.text: Maximum salary or wages = 5 × A × B ÷ 365, where A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends and B is the number of days in the taxation year in which the individual was a specified employee
(For example, in the CRA Guide T4088 illustration where the CPP YMPE was $43,700, the 5 × YMPE maximum per specified employee was $218,500)43.

items: Associated Corporations Allocation Agreement (Form T1174): If a specified employee works for two or more associated corporations, their salary or wages cannot be claimed by any of the corporations unless the corporations file an agreement using prescribed Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)) accompanied by a certified copy of the directors' resolution authorizing the agreement (or a signed confirmation by the sole shareholder if owned exclusively by one shareholder), ensuring the combined allocation across all associated corporations does not exceed 5 × YMPE38.

body.text: Permissible Salary or Wages for SR&ED Outside Canada (The 10% Cap – Subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5))

Under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) of the ITA, permissible salary or wages paid to employees for SR&ED work carried on outside Canada are deemed to be incurred in Canada if four conditions are met5:

items: The SR&ED work is performed directly by an employee of the claimant and not a contractor5;
The employee who performed the work was a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred5;
The foreign SR&ED work is related to the claimant's business and is carried on solely in support of SR&ED carried on by the taxpayer inside Canada5; and

The total permissible outside-Canada salary or wages claimed—split on Form T661 between non-specified employees (Line 307) and specified employees (Line 309)—cannot exceed 10% of the total amount of SR&ED salary or wages for SR&ED directly undertaken inside Canada (reported on Line 306 of Form T661, so that the maximum allowable on Line 309 is 10% of Line 306 minus Line 307; under the traditional method, the base for the 10% limit also includes non-directly-engaged employees whose tasks directly undertake, supervise, or support SR&ED reported on Line 360, excluding clerical staff providing general administrative support)5.

body.text: 3.3 The Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Calculation and Overall Cap

When a claimant elects the proxy method, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is computed in Part 5 of Form T661 under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations and the Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy (updated March 27, 2026)19. Since 2014 (after being reduced from 65% to 55% over a two-year period beginning in 2013), the PPA rate is 55% of the claimant's salary base, subject to an overall PPA cap12.
Step 1: Determining the Salary Base (Part 5, Section A of Form T661)

The salary base comprises the eligible portion of salaries or wages for employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (and permissible work outside Canada deemed incurred in Canada) that were incurred and paid in the taxation year or within 180 days of taxation year-end26. For all employees (both specified and non-specified), the salary base cannot include any of the following five items26:

items: Bonuses26;
Remuneration based on profits26;
Taxable benefits26;
Unpaid amounts from prior years that were paid in the current taxation year26; and
Employer contributions to related benefits (e.g., CPP/EI)26.

body.text: For non-specified employees, 100% of their eligible directly engaged SR&ED salary or wages (after the five exclusions above) is entered on Line 810 of Form T66126.
For each specified employee (reported in Part 5 on Lines 850 to 858 of Form T661), the amount included in the salary base is restricted to the lesser of two caps26:

items: The 75% Salary Cap: A maximum of 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages for the year (SR&ED and non-SR&ED combined, excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior years' unpaid salary/wages), multiplied by the percentage of time spent on SR&ED26; and

The 2.5 × YMPE Cap (Line 858): A maximum limit of 2.5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated for the number of days employed during the year26:

body.text: 2.5 × A × B ÷ 365, where A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends and B is the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual

If a specified employee is employed by associated corporations in taxation years ending in the same calendar year, the combined total salary included in the salary base across the associated entities cannot exceed 2.5 × YMPE and must be shared among the associated corporations26.
Step 2: Applying the 55% Rate and the Overall Cap on PPA

The total salary base is multiplied by 55% on Line 820 of Form T66126. To ensure that total qualified SR&ED expenditures, the PPA, and allowed statutory deductions do not exceed overall business expenditures, an Overall Cap may limit the calculated PPA (though it usually does not restrict the PPA if the claimant has deducted more than $55 of non-SR&ED operating expenses for each $100 of eligible salary in the salary base)26. The Overall Cap formula (combined across all businesses if the claimant operates more than one business) is26:
Overall Cap on PPA = A − B − C
Where:

items: A is the total amounts deducted when calculating net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including Cost of Goods Sold)26;

B is the sum of specific deductions claimed under Section 20 (e.g., Capital Cost Allowance [CCA], interest, bad debts), Section 24 (cessation of business), Section 26 (banks), Section 30 (farming land improvement), Section 32 (insurance agents/brokers), Section 37 (SR&ED expenditures claimed on Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1), Sections 66 to 66.8 (exploration and development expenses), and Section 104 (trusts)26; and
C is the total expenditures incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building26.

body.text: 3.4 Overhead and Other Expenditures Under the Traditional Method

Claimants using the traditional method may claim SR&ED overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661 pursuant to clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) of the ITA and subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3) of the Income Tax Regulations19.
The Dual "Directly Related" and "Incremental" Tests

Under paragraph 2900(2)(c) and paragraph 2900(3)(b) of the Regulations, and per the CRA SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy (updated October 14, 2022), an overhead expenditure (or a reasonably allocated portion thereof) qualifies only if it is directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (or to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for SR&ED), which requires satisfying two cumulative tests19:

items: The "Directly Related" Test: The expenditure must be directly related to the prosecution ("to carry on; engage in") of SR&ED in Canada, meaning there must be a direct linkage (with no intervening step or intermediary) to the SR&ED work, to the SR&ED staff, or to the machinery/equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED44. Any indirect portion must be excluded, and a rational, reasonable method must be used to allocate the expense45.
The "Incremental" Test: The expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred44.

body.text: Applying these two tests, the CRA allows the employer's share of related benefits for employees who directly undertake, supervise, or support SR&ED because it has a direct link to SR&ED work44. By contrast, the employer's share of related benefits for clerical and administrative staff who support SR&ED employees is disallowed because it has only an indirect link to the SR&ED work (even when those clerical employees' incremental salaries themselves qualify as overhead on Line 360)44. Moving expenses to relocate SR&ED candidates or employees, taxable benefits related to hiring SR&ED personnel, incremental training and travel costs, and retiring allowances directly related and incremental to SR&ED may also be claimed under the traditional method19. Conversely, fixed monthly payments for telephone, cellular, or internet services and fixed-cost maintenance contracts fail the incremental test and are disallowed (though identifiable long-distance telephone charges directly related and incremental to SR&ED may qualify)45. Costs for waste disposal after an SR&ED activity has finished generally do not qualify unless the scrap is recycled and reused in SR&ED, in which case disposal costs form part of the material cost45.
Treatment of Cloud Computing, SaaS Subscriptions, Software, and Data Costs
A frequent issue for technology companies is how the CRA treats cloud computing (such as AWS, Azure, or GCP), SaaS subscriptions, software licences, and datasets46:

items: Unlike the United Kingdom (which introduced a specific qualifying R&D expenditure category for cloud computing services and data licences for accounting periods beginning on or after April 1, 2023), Canada’s SR&ED legislation does not list cloud computing or SaaS subscriptions as a standalone qualifying expenditure category47.

Under the Proxy Method, cloud computing and SaaS subscriptions cannot be claimed on Form T661 because they fall outside the statutory proxy categories (directly engaged salaries, materials consumed/transformed, 80% of Canadian contracts/third-party payments, and post-December 15, 2024 capital/equipment leases); instead, they are covered by the 55% PPA and deducted as ordinary business expenses19.

Under the Traditional Method, incremental usage-based cloud computing or hosting expenses incurred exclusively to run SR&ED experiments may only be claimed on Line 360 if the claimant can substantiate that they pass both the "directly related" and "incremental" tests under paragraph 2900(2)(c)45.

Software and Data Purchases as Capital: Computer software and software licences whose useful life is anticipated to last beyond one year, as well as purchases of enduring data, are treated by the CRA as capital expenditures of an enduring nature rather than current material expenditures1. For property acquired after December 15, 2024, depreciable software meeting the ASA (90% or more) SR&ED usage test may be evaluated under the restored SR&ED capital expenditure rules, whereas non-depreciable data purchases do not qualify1.

body.text: Prescribed Excluded Expenditures (Regulation 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations)
Under Regulation 2902, prescribed expenditures are excluded from qualified expenditures and never earn ITCs (deducted on Line 530 / Line 532 of Form T661)9. Prescribed excluded expenditures include:

items: General administration or management expenses, including legal or accounting fees, interest and financing costs, advertising, entertainment, fines or penalties, and membership dues21;

Administrative salaries or wages for employees who do not devote all or substantially all (90% or more) of their time to SR&ED (unless directly related and incremental under the traditional method)21;
Maintenance and upkeep costs for premises or facilities not attributable to SR&ED prosecution21;
Fees paid for preparing SR&ED claims or attending conventions and conferences21;
Expenditures made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED (paragraph 2902(c))6; and
Capital expenditures for the acquisition or refurbishment of used depreciable property9.

body.text: 3.5 Materials Consumed and Materials Transformed

Under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) of the ITA (proxy method) and paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Regulations (traditional method), a claimant may claim 100% of the cost of materials consumed or materials transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada19.
The Tangible Object and "Body of a Thing" Requirement

Per the CRA Materials for SR&ED Policy (updated December 18, 2014), "materials for SR&ED" means all the raw materials, substances, or other physical and tangible items (generally in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that compose the body of a "thing" (a tangible object) at a given moment in the SR&ED process29. Specifically, items qualify as materials for SR&ED only if, at a given moment in the SR&ED process, they compose the body of either (1) a tangible object on which the SR&ED is being carried out, or (2) a tangible object that results from the SR&ED being carried out (including tangible objects involved in testing a new or improved process)51.

For example, in a laboratory and field plant-science project, seeds, growth media, agar, fungal cultures, and fertilizers, pesticides, and herbicides applied to test plots compose the body of the thing on which SR&ED is performed and qualify as materials consumed51. By contrast, broken or used lab supplies (petri dishes, beakers, flasks, pipettes), cleaning supplies, CDs/DVDs, used lubricants such as engine oil, and general utilities (water, electricity, oil, natural gas, propane, or steam used for energy) do not compose the body of the object under investigation and do not qualify as materials for SR&ED (though they may qualify as Line 360 overhead under the traditional method)51.

Materials may be purchased from Canadian or foreign suppliers and are claimed only in the taxation year in which they are actually consumed or transformed in SR&ED in Canada42. For purchased goods, the claimable cost is the laid-down cost, which includes the invoice cost, customs and excise duties, transportation, storage, and other acquisition or processing costs required to bring the item to its condition and location to be consumed or transformed in SR&ED (for instance, where metal parts must be galvanized by a contractor before destructive SR&ED testing, both the metal cost and the galvanization service cost form the claimable cost of materials consumed)51. For internally manufactured inventory, the cost includes laid-down materials, direct labour, and a share of production overhead51. For purchases from non-arm's-length suppliers, the ITC earned is restricted to the actual cost incurred by the non-arm's-length supplier, excluding any intercompany profit margin21.
Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed

items: Materials Consumed: "Consumed" means absorbed, used up, or broken down into small pieces—meaning the material was destroyed or rendered virtually valueless as a result of the SR&ED29. Under the CRA 90% rule, if 90% or more of the cost/value of the material was consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED, the entire cost of the material is allowable as materials consumed, and no ITC recapture applies34. Conversely, if experimental production is sold for more than 10% of its original cost, it is not considered consumed51.

Materials Transformed: When materials for SR&ED are not rendered virtually valueless after the SR&ED process (retaining value or being recycled/reused, or forming a component part incorporated into a custom product or commercial asset), they are treated as materials transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED34. While 100% of the cost of materials transformed is deductible under Section 37 and earns an ITC under Section 127 in the year transformed, materials transformed are subject to SR&ED ITC recapture under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) if the resulting property is later sold or converted to commercial use within 20 taxation years34.

body.text: Prototypes, Pilot Plants, Commercial Plants, and Custom Assets
Per the CRA SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy (July 19, 2016), physical assets developed or used during R&D fall into four categories52:

items: Prototypes: A prototype is an original trial model possessing the essential characteristics of the intended product, developed to test the feasibility of a concept or hypothesis and typically having no lasting commercial value52. Labour and materials used in designing, constructing, and testing a prototype (as well as duplicate copies of a prototype constructed and damaged during pre-commercial line testing) qualify as current SR&ED expenditures (materials consumed or, if retaining value, materials transformed subject to recapture)52. Constructing duplicate copies to meet market demand or build commercial inventory does not qualify52.

Pilot Plants: A pilot plant is a non-commercial scale production facility developed for the primary purpose of carrying out SR&ED during its useful life and never converted to commercial operations52. Labour and materials consumed or transformed in resolving technological uncertainties or operating the pilot plant (resulting in "experimental production") qualify as current SR&ED expenditures52.

Commercial Plants and Custom Products / Commercial Assets: When SR&ED is performed while developing or modifying a commercial plant or a custom commercial asset, claimants must separate SR&ED costs from commercial costs52. Where it is impossible to isolate SR&ED work from commercial work on a custom product or commercial asset, the CRA offers an Alternative Approach formula:

body.text: Allowable SR&ED expenditures = (total actual costs of developing the custom product or commercial asset − estimated costs that would usually be associated with constructing the asset if the technology had already existed) + estimated cost of materials transformed in SR&ED

Using this formula requires mutual agreement with the CRA and requires the claimant to sign a formal waiver of the right to object or appeal under subsection 169(2.2) of the ITA52. (For example, if a machine with an experimental engine costs $150,000 in total, would have cost $125,000 using existing technology, and includes $30,000 of materials transformed in SR&ED, the allowable SR&ED expenditure is ($150,000 − $125,000) + $30,000 = $55,000, subject to ITC recapture)52.
3.6 Subcontractor Payments (SR&ED Contracts) and Third-Party Payments

The Income Tax Act distinguishes between contract expenditures for SR&ED performed on behalf of a claimant (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01)) and third-party payments (subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii))5.
1. Arm's-Length SR&ED Contracts (The 80% ITC Rule)

Per the CRA Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy (updated March 30, 2022), when a claimant contracts an arm's-length party to perform basic research, applied research, experimental development, or eligible paragraph 248(1)(d) support work on behalf of the claimant in Canada, 100% of the eligible contract expenditure enters the Section 37 deductible pool, and 80% of the expenditure qualifies for the Section 127 ITC (reported on Line 370 of Form T661, with 20% deducted on Line 529)12.
Four mandatory rules govern arm's-length SR&ED contracts:

items: Performed in Canada: Expenditures for SR&ED contract work performed outside Canada cannot be claimed on Form T661 and do not earn an ITC (though current expenditures for foreign contracts may be deducted in computing net business income under subsection 37(2))5;

Taxable Supplier Requirement: For ITC purposes, the payment must be made to a "taxable supplier" (as defined in subsection 127(9)); amounts paid or payable to a non-taxable supplier are deducted on Line 528 of Form T661 and earn 0% ITC21;

"On Behalf Of" and Contract Payment Deduction by Performer: To determine whether SR&ED was performed "on behalf of" a payer, the CRA evaluates (a) whether the contractor is obligated under the contract to perform specific SR&ED tasks; (b) pricing versus who bears the financial and technical risk of failure; (c) whether the payer retains commercial ownership of the resulting intellectual property (IP); and (d) whether the contract is for services rather than the sale of goods12. To avoid duplication of ITCs, the payment is a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9) that reduces the contractor's (performer's) own qualified SR&ED expenditures12; and

Contracts for Support Work Only: Where a claimant contracts out only paragraph 248(1)(d) support work to an arm's-length party, the payer may claim the contract expenditure (under both the traditional and proxy methods) provided the support work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of basic research, applied research, or experimental development performed in Canada by or on behalf of the payer25. The arm's-length performer cannot claim expenditures for support-only work because support work on its own does not meet the definition of SR&ED25. (Contract costs for non-SR&ED work, such as work by electricians, welders, or mechanics that is not paragraph 248(1)(d) support work, may qualify only under the traditional method as Line 360 overhead if directly related and incremental)19.

body.text: 2. Non-Arm's Length (NAL) SR&ED Contracts and Form T1146 Transfers
Where a claimant (payer) enters into an SR&ED contract with a non-arm's length (NAL) performer:

items: Under subsection 37(13), work performed by a NAL performer (including support work only) is deemed to be SR&ED if it would be SR&ED had it been performed directly by the payer5.
However, the payer's contract expenditure is an allowable Section 37 expenditure but is excluded from qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsection 127(9) and earns 0% ITC for the payer21.
Instead, the amount received by the NAL performer is not considered a contract payment, so the NAL performer can claim its own underlying SR&ED expenditures and earn the ITC25.

Transferring Qualified Expenditures via Form T1146 (Subsection 127(13)): Under subsection 127(13), the NAL performer may transfer all or a portion of its qualified SR&ED expenditures (up to the contract amount) to the payer by filing prescribed Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) (updated May 15, 2026; reported on Line 508 by the transferee and Line 546 by the transferor on Form T661)9. Under subsection 127(24), anti-avoidance rules prevent a claimant from circumventing NAL contract exclusions by interposing an arm's-length party between the payer and a NAL subcontractor25.

body.text: 3. Third-Party Payments (Entities A to F and Form T1263)

Per the CRA Third-Party Payments Policy (updated March 30, 2022) and subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii) of the ITA, a third-party payment (in cash, student/employee funding, or payment in kind valued at fair market value) is a payment made to an eligible entity for SR&ED carried on in Canada that is related to a business of the claimant, where the claimant is entitled to exploit the results of the SR&ED5. Only 80% of a third-party payment (reported on Line 340 of Form T661, with 20% deducted on Line 529) qualifies for the Section 127 ITC21. Claimants must complete and attach Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED) for each payment42.
The CRA classifies eligible third-party entities into six categories5:

items: Entity A (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1)): A corporation resident in Canada (the SR&ED tax incentive on payments to an Entity A is earned only in the year the SR&ED is performed, rather than the year paid)5;
Entity B (Clause 37(1)(a)(ii)(A)): An approved association that undertakes SR&ED (earned in the year paid)5;
Entity C (Clause 37(1)(a)(ii)(B)): An approved university, college, research institute, or similar institution (earned in the year paid)5;
Entity D (Clause 37(1)(a)(ii)(C)): A non-profit SR&ED corporation resident in Canada and exempt from tax under paragraph 149(1)(j)5;
Entity E (Clause 37(1)(a)(ii)(E)): An approved organization (granting council) that makes payments to an Entity B, C, or D5; and

body.text: The 180-Day Unpaid Amount Rule for Non-Wage Current Expenditures (Subsection 127(26))

Under subsection 127(26) of the ITA, any current SR&ED expenditure other than salary or wages that remains unpaid within 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which it was incurred is deducted from qualified expenditures on Line 520 of Form T661 and is added back on Line 500 only in the subsequent taxation year when it is actually paid21. Crucially, the unpaid expenditure must be identified on Form T661 on or before the 18-month reporting deadline for the taxation year in which it was incurred; if not identified within that 18-month deadline, it can never be included in qualified SR&ED expenditures even when paid in a later year21. For an unpaid arm's-length SR&ED contract (e.g., $100,000), a 20% reduction ($20,000) is applied first on Line 529, the remaining 80% ($80,000) is deducted on Line 520 as an unpaid amount, and when paid in a subsequent year, 80% ($80,000) is entered on Line 50021.
3.7 Capital Expenditures, Equipment Leases, and Shared-Use Equipment (Post-December 15, 2024)

Under Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026), Parliament restored SR&ED tax incentives for capital expenditures, shared-use equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 (property acquired or lease costs first becoming payable on or after December 16, 2024)10. Any depreciable property acquired or lease cost incurred between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, does not qualify9.
1. SR&ED Capital Expenditures (Paragraph 37(1)(b) & ITR 2902(b))

Per the updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), an expenditure made after December 15, 2024, qualifies as an SR&ED capital expenditure (reported in Part 6B of Form T661) if it results in the acquisition of depreciable property (as defined in subsection 13(21) of the ITA, owned by the claimant and available for use under subsection 37(1.2)) that satisfies one of two All or Substantially All (ASA, 90% or more) intent tests5:

items: ASA Operating Time Test: The property is intended to be used during all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada9; or

ASA Value Consumed Test: All or substantially all (90% or more) of its value is intended to be consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada (for example, property used in developing an asset where the property has less than 10% life expectancy or less than 10% value remaining afterward, or continues to be used in other SR&ED)9.

body.text: Qualifying capital expenditures enter the Section 37 pool under paragraph 37(1)(b) and, when deducted under subsection 37(1), are deemed by subsection 37(6) to be Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) allowed under paragraph 20(1)(a) in a separate prescribed class5. However, while both new and used ASA depreciable property may be deducted in the Section 37 pool, the acquisition or refurbishment of used property is a prescribed expenditure under Regulation 2902 (deducted on Line 532 of Form T661) and does not qualify for a Section 127 ITC9. Furthermore, land, leasehold interests in land, inventory, and goodwill are non-depreciable and excluded5, and paragraph 37(8)(e) excludes any building or leasehold interest in a building other than a prescribed special-purpose building under Regulation 290320.
2. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) – First-Term and Second-Term 25% Rules

When new depreciable equipment acquired after December 15, 2024, is used for both SR&ED and commercial activities such that it does not meet the 90% ASA threshold, its capital cost is depreciated under normal CCA rules on Schedule T2SCH8 rather than entering the Section 37 pool9. However, under the definitions of "first term shared-use-equipment" and "second term shared-use-equipment" in subsection 127(9) of the ITA and the updated SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), the equipment earns a Section 127 ITC (reported on Line 504 and Part 6C Boxes 792/794 of Form T661) if its actual operating time is primarily (more than 50% but less than 90%) for SR&ED in Canada9:

items: Eligibility Requirements for SUE: The property must be (a) depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024; (b) new property (never used, acquired to be used, or rented for any purpose before acquisition); (c) not ASA (≥90%) SR&ED capital property; (d) not General-Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) (desks, chairs, lamps, filing cabinets, bookshelves, photocopiers, fax machines, telephones, pagers, and calculators); and (e) not Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under subsection 2900(11) of the Regulations10. Under subsection 2900(11), a property is excluded as PDP if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended to use it for SR&ED during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial manufacturing/processing facility and intended to use it primarily (>50%) for non-SR&ED purposes over its expected useful life10.

First-Term SUE (25% of Capital Cost): If the equipment is actually used >50% of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada during the First Period—which starts when the property is acquired (available for use) and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after that time—1/4 (25%) of the capital cost (excluding borrowed money costs and adjusted for NAL transfers under subsection 127(11.6) and assistance) is deemed to be a qualified expenditure for ITC purposes10.

Second-Term SUE (Additional 25% of Capital Cost): Provided the equipment qualified as First-Term SUE, if it is actually used >50% of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada during the Second Period—which starts when the property was acquired (available for use) and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after that time—an additional 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost (totalling 50% across both periods) qualifies for the ITC10. (For example, in Section 3.5 of the CRA SUE Policy, a $300,000 machine acquired on January 2, 2025, by a calendar-year taxpayer has less than 12 months of operating time on December 31, 2025; on December 31, 2026 [First Period, 81% SR&ED use], 25% or $75,000 qualifies as First-Term SUE; and on December 31, 2027 [Second Period, 66% SR&ED use], another 25% or $75,000 qualifies as Second-Term SUE)10.

body.text: 3. Equipment Lease Expenditures (Post-December 15, 2024)

Per the updated SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026), lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024, for equipment used in SR&ED in Canada (reported on Lines 350/355 and Part 6A Box 759 of Form T661) qualify as follows9:

items: Under the Traditional Method (Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I) and (II)):
When leased equipment is used ASA (90% or more) of its operating time in the year for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease expenditure is claimable as a lease cost36.

When leased equipment is used less than 90% of its operating time for SR&ED, a proportional percentage of the lease expenditure may be claimed on Line 360 as an overhead and other expenditure if directly related and incremental to SR&ED9.
Under the Proxy Method (Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) and (VI)):
When leased equipment (other than GPOEF) is used ASA (90% or more) of its operating time in the year for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease cost is claimable36.
When leased equipment (other than GPOEF) is used primarily (more than 50% to less than 90%) of its operating time in the year for SR&ED in Canada, 50% of the lease cost can be claimed36.
When leased equipment is used 50% or less of its operating time for SR&ED (or is GPOEF), 0% of the lease cost can be claimed under the proxy method36.

Building and Land Leases: Building rent is excluded under subparagraph 37(8)(d)(ii) except for a prescribed special-purpose building19. Leasing land after December 15, 2024, may be claimed as Line 360 overhead under the traditional method if ASA or directly attributable to SR&ED, but is not allowable under the proxy method36. Operating time is measured across the full 12-month taxation year (or for a transitional taxation year including December 16, 2024, across total operating time after December 15, 2024) and must be supported by equipment usage logs9.

body.text: 3.8 Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, Contract Payments, and ITC Recapture
Reduction of SR&ED Pools by Assistance and Contract Payments

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(18) and 127(19) of the ITA, and per the CRA Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, tax incentives are provided only on the net costs of performing SR&ED12. Accordingly, any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payment that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date of the income tax return is recognized on an accrual basis12:

items: Government Assistance (Subsection 127(9)): Includes grants, subsidies, forgivable loans (where repayment is contingent on future project revenues or profits), investment allowances, super-allowance benefit amounts, and provincial/territorial R&D tax credits (such as NRC IRAP grants or provincial credits)12. However, under the Bill C-69 amendment to subsection 127(9) (enacted June 20, 2024, retroactive to January 1, 2020), excluded loans (defined in subsection 12(11)) with reasonable repayment terms are not government assistance9.
Non-Government Assistance (Subsection 127(9) & Paragraph 12(1)(x)): Includes inducements, reimbursements, contributions, or allowances from non-government entities12.

Pool Impact & Form T1145 Allocation: Assistance reduces both the Section 37 deductible pool (on a project-by-project basis, never below zero; any excess is included in income) and Section 127 qualified expenditures, whereas contract payments reduce only Section 127 qualified expenditures12. Where the proxy method is used, the portion of a provincial R&D tax credit calculated on the PPA reduces federal Section 127 qualified expenditures, but does not reduce the federal Section 37 deductible pool (it is instead included in net income on Schedule T2SCH1 in the year received)12. Excess assistance within a non-arm's-length group is allocated under subsection 127(19) using Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) (updated May 15, 2026)9.

body.text: The 20-Year SR&ED ITC Recapture Window (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

Under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the ITA and the Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 14, 2022), all four of the following conditions trigger recapture of a previously earned SR&ED ITC34:

items: The claimant acquired a particular property from a person or partnership in the current taxation year or in any of the 20 preceding taxation years (subsection 127(36))34;

The cost of the property was a qualified SR&ED expenditure (materials transformed, ASA capital equipment, Shared-Use Equipment [SUE], animals/growing things, or property acquired via an arm's-length SR&ED contract)34;
A percentage of the property's cost was included in computing the claimant's ITC34; and
In the taxation year, the claimant disposes of the property or converts it to commercial use (for SUE, when sold or when all or substantially all of the property is converted to commercial use)10.

body.text: Recapture is calculated by multiplying the applicable ITC rate at which the credit was originally earned by the lesser of (a) the proceeds of disposition (or fair market value upon conversion to commercial use) and (b) the original cost / qualified expenditure of the property, adding that amount directly to tax payable for the year (and adding it back to the Section 37 deductible pool in the following year under paragraph 37(1)(c.2))5. Internal salaries, wages, overhead, materials consumed, scrap sales under the de minimis rule, property not acquired from a person/partnership (such as animals born on a farm), and sales of intellectual property (IP) are not subject to ITC recapture34.
