body.text: 4.2 Ontario: OITC, OBRITC, and ORDTC

Ontario operates three corporate R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (S.O. 2007, c. 11, Sched. A), all administered by the CRA and requiring that the corporation maintain a permanent establishment in Ontario and carry on eligible SR&ED within Ontario14.

First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC – Section 96, Schedule 566) is an 8% fully refundable tax credit (reduced from 10% for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016) available to CCPCs on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000 (generating a maximum annual cash refund of $240,000, shared among associated corporations and prorated for short taxation years)13. Unlike the federal SR&ED expenditure limit (which doubled to $6 million under Bill C-15 for taxation years starting after December 15, 2024), Ontario’s OITC limit remains capped at $3 million13. The $3 million OITC expenditure limit is reduced under two prior-year phase-out grinds: (1) it begins to reduce once prior-year federal taxable income of the corporation and its associated group exceeds $500,000, reaching nil at $800,000; and (2) it begins to reduce once prior-year specified capital reaches $25,000,000, reaching nil at $50,000,00013. The OITC may be waived in whole or in part under subsection 96(14) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), and is claimed on Schedule 566 and entered on Line 468 of Schedule 514.

Second, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC – Section 97, Schedules 568 and 569) provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit to qualifying corporations on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred under an eligible contract with an Eligible Research Institute (ERI) in Ontario—including Ontario universities, Ontario colleges of applied arts and technology, hospital research institutes, and Ontario Centres of Excellence and Networks of Centres of Excellence14. The annual qualified expenditure limit is $20,000,000 (allocated among associated corporations), for a maximum credit of $4,000,000 per year14. Payments in kind and expenditures funding salaries of ERI employees connected to the claimant corporation are excluded17. Claimants file Schedule 568 along with a separate Schedule 569 for each eligible contract, entering the credit on Line 470 of Schedule 514.

Third, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC – Sections 38 to 45, Schedule 508) is a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (reduced from 4.5% for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016) available to all corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures13. Unused ORDTC credits carry back 3 years and carry forward 20 years to reduce Ontario corporate income tax otherwise payable13. A corporation can waive the ORDTC in whole or in part under subsection 43(1) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario)13. The ORDTC is claimed on Schedule 508 and entered on Line 416 of Schedule 5 (with any ORDTC recapture under section 45 reported on Line 277 of Schedule 5)13.
Step-by-Step Multi-Tier Stacking Calculation (Ontario CCPC + Federal SR&ED)

Because the OITC is treated as government assistance for ORDTC purposes, and both the OITC and ORDTC are treated as government assistance for federal SR&ED purposes under subsection 127(18) of the ITA, the credits are calculated in a three-step sequence14. Consider an Ontario CCPC with $1,000,000 of eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (all within its $3M OITC and $6M federal limits, with no grants)59:

items: Step 1 – Calculate OITC (8%): Applying 8% to the $1,000,000 OITC base yields an $80,000 refundable OITC59.

Step 2 – Calculate ORDTC (3.5%): Reducing the $1,000,000 base by the $80,000 OITC leaves an ORDTC base of $920,000; multiplying $920,000 by 3.5% yields a $32,200 non-refundable ORDTC (total Ontario credits = $112,200, or an effective 11.22% rate)59.

Step 3 – Calculate Federal SR&ED ITC (35%): Reducing the $1,000,000 federal qualified expenditure base by both the $80,000 OITC and the $32,200 ORDTC leaves a net federal base of $887,800; multiplying $887,800 by 35% yields a $310,730 refundable federal ITC59. (Similarly, on a $500,000 eligible Ontario expenditure pool, the 8% OITC is $40,000, the 3.5% ORDTC on the remaining $460,000 is $16,100, and the 35% federal ITC on the remaining $443,900 is $155,365)59. When the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount is included in a salary-based claim, the combined federal and Ontario credits return roughly 62% to 66% of eligible directly engaged SR&ED salary, with ~62% arriving in cash from the federal ITC plus the 8% OITC14.

body.text: 4.3 Québec: The 2025–2026 CRIC Overhaul, CDAEIA, C3i, and DICI

In the 2025–2026 Québec Budget presented on March 25, 2025 (and set out in Québec Finance Bulletin 2025-6 and Revenu Québec official guidance), the Government of Québec replaced its fragmented legacy R&D credits with a unified tax incentive architecture15.
Elimination of Legacy Québec R&D Tax Measures

For taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec eliminated the following legacy R&D and innovation tax measures (which remain claimable only for taxation years or fiscal periods beginning before March 26, 2025, where the legacy R&D salary and research credits provided a 14% base rate and up to a 30% SME enhanced rate)16:

items: The tax credit for salaries and wages of researchers16;
The tax credit for university research or research carried out by a public research centre or a research consortium16;
The tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium16;
The tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research16;
The tax credit for technological adaptation services16;
The industrial design component of the design tax credits (while expenditures for the fashion design component continue to be eligible)16; and
The tax holidays for foreign researchers and foreign experts (bringing the total to eight eliminated legacy measures)16.

body.text: The Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC)

Effective for taxation years or partnership fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, the CRIC (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation) is a 100% refundable corporate tax credit claimed by filing Form RD-1029.8.CR-T with the Québec corporate income tax return (CO-17)15:

items: Two-Tier Rate Structure (Independent of Company Size): Regardless of a corporation's asset size, the CRIC pays a refundable credit of 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures exceeding the applicable exclusion threshold, and 20% on qualified expenditures above that $1,000,000 maximum15.

Eligible R&D and Pre-Commercialization Activities: While Québec's R&D definition is harmonized with the federal SR&ED definition of basic research, applied research, and experimental development (with the CRA performing the scientific review of R&D work), the CRIC also covers pre-commercialization activities undertaken in Québec in conjunction with (and as a continuation of) R&D work carried out in Québec by or on behalf of the corporation15. Eligible pre-commercialization activities consist of: (1) tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements aimed at obtaining an initial approval or certification for commercializing an innovation (quality control is eligible only if it relates to implementing a quality control system required for initial approval or certification); and (2) product design, including the development of form/shape and aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials15.

Qualified Expenditures: Qualified expenditures incurred in Québec comprise: (1) 100% of salaries and wages paid to the corporation's employees for eligible R&D and pre-commercialization work; (2) 50% of amounts paid to a subcontractor for an eligible contract carried out in Québec; (3) 50% of payments made to an eligible public research centre, eligible research consortium, or eligible university entity in Québec; and (4) 100% of property acquisition costs (capital expenditures) for new depreciable equipment used in R&D or pre-commercialization in Québec, excluding costs relating to the acquisition of a building, land, or a right to use a building or land15.

Applicable Exclusion Threshold: Qualified expenditures in a taxation year must exceed an exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the basic personal amount of the applicable personal income tax system for each employee ($18,571 in 2025), adjusted to reflect the percentage of time spent by each employee on eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities15.

Non-Cumulation Rules: Government and non-government financial assistance must be subtracted from qualified expenditures, and a corporation cannot claim both the CRIC and another Québec tax credit (such as the C3i credit) on the same expenditure, nor claim property used under a large investment project tax holiday15.

items: CDAE and Replacement by CDAEIA (After December 31, 2025): Québec's e-business development tax credit (CDAE)—which provided a 30% credit on eligible IT salaries (24% refundable + 6% non-refundable in 2024; 23% refundable + 7% non-refundable in 2025; requiring an annual Investissement Québec certificate, at least 6 full-time eligible employees, ≥75% IT revenue, ≥50% software development/publishing revenue, and ≥75% eligible employee duties, with the $100,000 salary cap replaced after December 31, 2024, by an exclusion threshold)—is replaced by the CDAEIA for fiscal years starting after December 31, 202557. Investment and Innovation Tax Credit (C3i): Provides a fully refundable credit (for tax years beginning after 2023) of 15%, 20%, or 25% by region on manufacturing or processing equipment, computer hardware, and management software acquired after March 10, 2020, and before January 1, 2030, on costs above $5,000 or $12,500 per property up to a $100 million 4-year cumulative cap57.

Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (DICI): Reduces the Québec corporate income tax rate from 11.5% to 2% on eligible income from commercializing qualified intellectual property assets (patents, pending applications, certificates of supplementary protection, or copyrighted software) resulting from Québec R&D57. body.text: 4.4 Western, Atlantic, and Northern Jurisdictions

items: British Columbia (BC SR&ED Tax Credit – Form T666): Under Sections 97 to 103 of the Income Tax Act (British Columbia), BC provides a 10% tax credit on SR&ED qualified BC expenditures17. For CCPCs, the credit is refundable up to 10% of the $3,000,000 expenditure limit (maximum refund of $300,000, phasing out over prior-year taxable capital from $10 million to $50 million)7. For non-CCPCs and CCPC amounts above the limit, the 10% credit is non-refundable and may be carried back 3 years and carried forward 10 years17. Form T666 must be filed within 18 months after the corporation's tax year-end17.

Alberta (Innovation Employment Grant [IEG] – AT1 Schedule 29 & Form AT4970): Under Sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act (for expenditures incurred after December 31, 2020), the IEG provides qualified corporations with a fully refundable grant on up to $4,000,000 in annual Alberta R&D spending: an 8% payment on eligible spending up to the corporation's base spending level (the average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the previous 2 years) and an enhanced 20% payment on eligible spending exceeding that base level17. The filing deadline is 15 months after the corporation's filing-due date17.

Saskatchewan (Schedule T2SCH403): Under Sections 63 to 63.4 of The Income Tax Act (Saskatchewan), CCPCs earn a 10% refundable credit on eligible expenditures up to a $1,000,000 annual limit, and a 10% non-refundable credit on expenditures exceeding $1,000,00017. Other corporations earn a 10% non-refundable credit on all eligible expenditures17. Non-refundable credits carry back 3 years and forward 10 years17.

Manitoba (Schedule T2SCH380): Under Section 7.3 of The Income Tax Act (Manitoba), corporations earn a 15% tax credit on eligible Manitoba expenditures17. For in-house R&D, one-half (7.5%) is refundable and the remaining 7.5% is non-refundable (carrying back 3 years and forward 20 years)17. R&D carried on under contract with a qualifying institute in Manitoba is 100% refundable (15%), and contract payments to eligible educational institutions in Manitoba are 100% eligible rather than 80%17. The filing deadline is 1 year after the filing-due date17.

New Brunswick (Schedule T2SCH360), Nova Scotia (Schedule T2SCH340), Newfoundland and Labrador (Schedule T2SCH301), and Yukon (Schedule T2SCH442 / Form T1232): All four jurisdictions provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit administered by the CRA17. New Brunswick's credit (Section 59 of the New Brunswick Income Tax Act) has a filing deadline of 15 months after the corporation's filing-due date17. Nova Scotia's credit (Section 41 of the Income Tax Act (Nova Scotia)) has a filing deadline of 18 months after the corporation's tax year-end, applies recapture, and can be renounced within 6 months of year-end17. Newfoundland and Labrador's credit (Section 42 of the Income Tax Act (Newfoundland and Labrador)) is available to corporations, individuals, trusts, and partnerships within 12 months after the filing-due date, and its eligible expenditure base is not reduced by government or non-government assistance (except GST/HST input tax credits)17. Yukon's credit (Section 15 of the Income Tax Act (Yukon)) is available to corporations, individuals, trusts, and partnerships within 12 months after the filing-due date at 15% refundable, plus an additional 5% refundable credit (20% total) on amounts paid or payable to Yukon University17.

body.text: 5. Governance, Filing Procedures, Audit Protocols, and Dispute Resolution
5.1 Governing Authorities and Statutory Filing Deadlines

The federal SR&ED legislation is the responsibility of the Department of Finance Canada, while the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers the program, evaluates technical and financial claims, and manages the pre-claim approval process1. Under subsection 37(3) of the ITA, the Minister may also obtain technical advice from the Department of Industry, the National Research Council of Canada, the Defence Research Board, or other government agencies to determine whether an activity constitutes SR&ED5.
Absolute Statutory Reporting Deadlines (Subsections 37(11) and 127(9))

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of subsection 127(9) of the ITA, and per the CRA SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy (updated January 28, 2025), prescribed forms containing prescribed information must be filed on or before the SR&ED reporting deadline, which is 12 months after the filing-due date of the income tax return for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred5:

items: Corporations (18 Months After Tax Year-End): A corporation's T2 income tax return filing-due date is 6 months after its taxation year-end; adding 12 months results in an SR&ED reporting deadline of 18 months after the end of the taxation year27. (For example, for a March 31, 2022 tax year-end, the T2 return is due September 30, 2022, and the SR&ED reporting deadline is September 30, 2023)71.

Individuals and Partnerships (17.5 Months After Calendar Year-End): An individual's business T1 return is due June 15 of the following year; adding 12 months results in an SR&ED reporting deadline of 17.5 months after calendar year-end (June 15 of the second following year)43.

Trusts (15 Months After Tax Year-End): A trust's T3 return is due 90 days (approximately 3 months) after its taxation year-end; adding 12 months results in an SR&ED reporting deadline of 15 months after the end of the taxation year54.
Non-Profit SR&ED Corporations (6 Months After Tax Year-End): Must file Form T661 within 6 months after the end of the taxation year (and cannot claim an ITC)71.

body.text: Consequences of Late or Incomplete Filing (Subsections 37(11.1), 37(12), and 220(2.2))

Under subsections 37(11.1) and 37(12) of the ITA, if the prescribed forms and prescribed information are not filed on or before the SR&ED reporting deadline, no amount may be deducted under subsection 37(1), the expenditure is deemed not to be an SR&ED expenditure, and no ITC is allowed5. If Form T661 is filed on time, but Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND) is filed after the SR&ED reporting deadline, the claimant may still deduct the allowable SR&ED expenditures in its Section 37 pool, but is not entitled to earn any ITC on those expenditures71. Pursuant to subsection 220(2.2) of the ITA, requests to waive or extend filing requirements under subsection 220(2.1) cannot be made in respect of prescribed forms or prescribed information for SR&ED72. A letter expressing an "intent to file" or a partial estimate does not satisfy the statutory filing requirements71. Filing at least 90 days before the SR&ED reporting deadline gives the CRA time to perform an initial review and notify the claimant of any deficiencies before the deadline expires71.
5.2 Prescribed Forms, Schedules, and Part 9 Claim Preparer Penalties

To access both SR&ED incentives, claimants must submit Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) (updated May 15, 2026) and Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) (updated May 22, 2026) or Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)), alongside any required supplementary forms (T1145, T1146, T1174, T1263, and Schedule T2SCH49)9.
Form T661 is structured into ten parts41:

items: Part 1 – General Information (Lines 010 to 157): Business name, 15-character Business Number (BN), tax year dates, total number of projects (Line 050), financial contact (Lines 100–110), technical contact (Lines 115–125), and partnership details41.

Part 2 – Project Information (Sections A, B, and C): Technical narratives and project details (including the new 2026 fields for the Canada Research and Development Classification [CRDC] research code and Pre-Claim Approval case numbers)7. Claimants may choose to submit Part 2 at the time of filing for only the 20 largest projects in dollar value, provided they include the costs of every claimed project in Part 6 and maintain completed Part 2 forms for all claimed projects at their place of business to provide to the CRA upon request (failure to provide them results in disallowance of the project expenditures)71. For projects designated by a federal agency as "classified information" for national security reasons, the claimant completes Part 2 Section B on a separate sheet kept on file (not submitted with the tax return) and includes a copy of the notification letter to the CRA with Form T66141.

Part 3 – Calculation of SR&ED Expenditures (Sections A, B, and C): Section A records the irrevocable annual method election (Traditional vs. Proxy); Section B computes allowable SR&ED expenditures (Lines 300 to 390); and Section C computes the Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures (Lines 420 to 470)21.

Part 4 – Calculation of Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for ITC Purposes (Lines 500 to 559): Computes total qualified SR&ED expenditures on Line 559 by adding prior years' unpaid amounts paid in the year (Line 500), the PPA (Line 502), Shared-Use Equipment (Line 504), and transferred NAL qualified expenditures (Line 508), and subtracting assistance/contract payments (including Line 518), current non-wage amounts unpaid within 180 days (Line 520), payments to non-taxable suppliers (Line 528), the 20% reduction on Line 340 third-party payments and Line 370 arm's-length contracts (Line 529), prescribed expenditures not allowed by regulations (Line 530 / Line 532), other deductions for non-taxable income (Line 533 / Line 535), assistance allocated via Form T1145 (Line 540), NAL supplier adjustments (Line 543), and qualified expenditures transferred via Form T1146 (Line 546)9.
Part 5 – Calculation of Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) (Sections A and B, Lines 810 to 858): Computes the salary base and the 55% PPA for claimants electing the proxy method41.

Part 6 – Project Costs (Parts 6A, 6B, and 6C): Records project-by-project costs for all projects claimed in the year, including Box 759 in Part 6A for post-December 15, 2024 equipment lease costs, Part 6B for post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures, and Part 6C (Boxes 792 and 794) for the 20 most expensive post-December 15, 2024 Shared-Use Equipment acquisitions9.

Parts 7, 8, 9, and 10 – Additional Information, Checklist, Claim Preparer Information, and Certification: Part 9 requires prescribed information for every claim preparer that accepted consideration to prepare or assist in preparing the claim (if no claim preparer assisted, only Lines 935, 970, and 975 are completed)71. Part 9 information is not subject to the SR&ED reporting deadline and an error or omission in Part 9 will not disallow the SR&ED claim; however, under subsection 162(5.3) of the ITA, a $1,000 penalty may be assessed if Part 9 claim preparer or billing arrangement information is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally, or solidarily, liable5. Overstated claims are also subject to the CRA Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025)9. Part 10 contains the mandatory certification by an authorized signing officer71.

body.text: 5.3 Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched the optional Pre-Claim Approval Process announced in Budget 2025, enabling eligible businesses to obtain a formal determination of whether their proposed R&D projects qualify for SR&ED tax incentives before commencing work or incurring costs7:

items: Eligibility: Open to small and medium-sized businesses (CCPCs, other Canadian corporations, or partnerships) with gross business income under $25,000,000 that are in good compliance standing with the CRA7.

Application & 8-Week Service Standard: Submitted online via Form T1322 through My Business Account before work begins; the CRA provides a pre-claim approval determination within eight weeks (8 weeks) and can approve project work eligibility for up to 3 years in advance7. Businesses can also book one-on-one information sessions with CRA officers9.

Post-Filing Review Rules (90-Day Expenditure-Only Track): Submitting an SR&ED claim (Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31) after year-end remains mandatory3. If a filed claim contains projects granted pre-claim approval, the CRA may select the claim for an expenditure-only review and will generally process it within 90 calendar days of receiving the complete claim78. Only if the CRA finds that the actual projects differed significantly from what was initially approved (or if the claim includes unapproved projects) will the CRA conduct a full review of both the work and expenditures under standard processing timelines78.

body.text: 5.4 CRA Technical and Financial Claim Review Process

All SR&ED claims undergo risk assessment (and random sampling)78. Once a claim is selected for review, the claimant cannot withdraw the claim because the certification on Form T661 cannot be revoked78. Per The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated April 20, 2026), reviews are conducted by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (who evaluates work eligibility and reports to a Research and Technology Manager [RTM]) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (who evaluates expenditure allowability and reports to a Financial Review Manager [FRM])72. Most reviews are conducted virtually via videoconferencing and electronic document sharing, with on-site visits considered on an exceptional, case-by-case basis78.
The review follows a three-step process78:

items: Step 1 – Start of the Review: The reviewer telephones the claimant to announce the selection, introduce the RTA and FR, confirm official language and contact details, explain the identified technical or financial issues and projects under review, and schedule a review meeting78.

Step 2 – Review Meeting and Supporting Evidence: The RTA and FR interview key technical and financial personnel, conduct a virtual or physical premises tour, and examine contemporaneous, dated supporting evidence (test records, photographs, videos, scrap, artifacts, financial statements, ledgers, journals, vouchers, receipts, and contracts), sharing preliminary findings at the end of the meeting78.

Step 3 – End of the Review, Proposal Package, and 30-Day Response Window: The RTA prepares the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report, which the FR uses to compute financial adjustments78. If adjustments are proposed, the CRA sends a Proposal Package containing the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report, a proposal letter summarizing proposed adjustments to expenditures, ITCs, and any penalties, and detailed adjustment schedules78. In accordance with the CRA's Standard Timelines for Information Requests, the claimant generally has 30 days from the date of the proposal letter to submit written representations, additional factual information, or supporting documents before the CRA issues its final letter and Notice of Assessment or Reassessment78.

body.text: 5.5 Four-Tier Dispute Resolution Escalation and Tax Court Appeals
Per the CRA Guidelines for Resolving Claimants' SR&ED Concerns (updated December 5, 2025), claimants have four sequential avenues to resolve disputes72:

items: Step 1 – Talk to the Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and/or Financial Reviewer (FR): Openly discuss factual misunderstandings and provide additional documentation directly to the RTA and/or FR before the file is closed72.

Step 2 – Contact the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and/or Financial Review Manager (FRM): If unresolved after Step 1, escalate to the RTM and/or FRM, who will review the facts and perspectives of both the claimant and the reviewers72.

Step 3 – Request an Administrative Review (Form RC532 to the Assistant Director): If concerns remain unresolved after Steps 1 and 2 and the claimant has received the Proposal Package, the claimant should inform the reviewers of its intent before the 30-day proposal period expires and submit Form RC532 (Request for Administrative Review) to the National SR&ED Administrative Review Intake Centre (Business Tax Incentives Directorate, Enterprise Building 13th Floor, 427 Laurier Ave W, Ottawa, ON K1A 0L5) before the file is closed72. Forwarded within 3 business days to the local SR&ED Assistant Director, the Administrative Review is not a new technical review; it determines whether the claimant was given due process and whether the technical and financial reviews were consistent with current SR&ED legislation and policies (resulting in the decision being either maintained or reconsidered/reassigned)72.

Step 4 – Formal Notice of Objection (CRA Appeals Branch) and Appeal to the Tax Court of Canada: Within 90 days from the date of the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, the claimant may file a formal Notice of Objection online (via My Business Account or Represent a Client) or by mail using Form RC592 to the Chief of Appeals at the designated Appeals Intake Centre72. (Note: A "large corporation"—whose total taxable capital employed in Canada with related corporations exceeds $10 million at year-end—must reasonably describe each issue, specify the exact dollar relief sought for each issue, and pay 50% of the disputed amount while objecting, whereas regular taxpayers do not have to pay disputed taxes, interest, or penalties while awaiting review by the CRA Appeals Branch or the Tax Court of Canada)72. If the dispute is not resolved by the Appeals Officer, the claimant may appeal to the Tax Court of Canada (TCC), with further appeal to the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA)72.

body.text: 6. Judicial Precedents and Case Law Analysis
6.1 The Foundational Common Law Test: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (1998 TCC)

The foundational common law authority governing SR&ED eligibility in Canada is Judge Donald Bowman’s decision in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC), which evaluated physical hydraulic scale modelling projects and was expressly approved by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (1998 FCA, Docket A-710-96) and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada28. Noting that most scientific research in Canada involves gradual, incremental progress rather than spectacular breakthroughs, Judge Bowman held that SR&ED legislation must be given a fair, large, and liberal construction and interpretation that best ensures the attainment of its objects, and articulated the Five Criteria (Five-Question) Test28:

items: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? If the resolution of a problem is reasonably predictable using standard procedures or routine engineering—defined as "techniques, procedures and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field"—there is no technological uncertainty28.

Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? Judge Bowman set out a five-stage process: (a) observation of the subject matter of the problem; (b) formulation of a clear objective; (c) identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty; (d) formulation of a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty; and (e) methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses18. An integral part of SR&ED is identifying and resolving new technological uncertainties that arise as the research progresses28.

Did the procedures adopted accord with established and objective principles of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses? While intuitive creativity and genius may play a crucial role, they must operate within the total discipline of the scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement and experiment, and the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses18. What may appear routine and obvious after the event may not have been obvious before the work was undertaken28.

Did the process result in a technological advancement? A technological advance is an advancement in the general understanding for persons knowledgeable in the field (and does not cease to be an advance in Canada merely because a researcher elsewhere, such as in China, may have privately made the same advance if that work is not generally known)28. Crucially, the rejection of a hypothesis after testing is nonetheless an advance because it eliminates a hitherto untested hypothesis and reinforces the measure of technological uncertainty28.

Was a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results kept as the work progressed? Although not explicitly stated in the Act, keeping a detailed record of hypotheses, tests, and results as work progresses is implicit in the concept of the "scientific method" and the statutory phrase "systematic investigation"18.

body.text: 6.2 Evidentiary Standards and Repeatability: Sass Manufacturing (1988 TCC), Consoltex (1997 TCC), RIS-Christie (1998 FCA), and C.W. Agencies

In Sass Manufacturing Limited v. M.N.R., 88 D.T.C. 1363, [1988] 1 C.T.C. 2524, [1988] T.C.J. No. 409 (TCC), Judge Sarchuk held that systematic investigation requires more than informal trial and error and introduced an early "repeatability" documentation requirement81. Subsequently, in Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen (1997), 97 D.T.C. 724, [1997] 2 C.T.C. 2846 (TCC), Judge Bowman emphasized that the tax incentives for SR&ED are intended to encourage scientific research in Canada and must be interpreted liberally in light of industrial realities28.

In RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Her Majesty The Queen (1998 FCA, Docket A-710-96), Justice Robertson of the Federal Court of Appeal rejected Sass Manufacturing's mandatory "repeatability criterion" (which had required recorded documentation enabling third parties to replicate exact test parameters)81. The FCA held that: (1) while documentary evidence showing the logical connection between tests is the "sure-fire" way to establish systematic research, lack of documentary evidence is not automatically fatal if the taxpayer provides a plausible explanation (e.g., accidental destruction) or adduces credible testimonial evidence (as also confirmed in Formadrain Inc. and Les Abeilles); (2) once it is proven that testing occurred and a technological advancement resulted, a logical inference arises that the testing was carried out systematically in accordance with Regulation 2900; and (3) there is no requirement that a research project actually culminate in a successful technological advance, as excluding failed research would undermine entrepreneurship30. In C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, the Federal Court of Appeal reaffirmed the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria as the governing appellate standard30.
6.3 Distinguishing Systematic Investigation from Trial-and-Error and Routine Engineering: Jentel Manufacturing (2011 FCA 355) and Joel Theatrical Rigging (2017 TCC 6)

In Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261, aff'd 2011 FCA 355, Justice D'Arcy of the Tax Court (affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal) found that although the taxpayer had provided sufficient documentation and records showing how its design work progressed, none of its activities qualified as SR&ED because there was no technological uncertainty that could not be resolved by routine engineering and a lack of testing of formulated hypotheses—distinguishing the scientific method from random "trial and error"2.

In Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6 (CanLII), Justice Sommerfeldt disallowed SR&ED claims for two theatrical rigging projects (the 2008 Fire Curtain Project and the 2009 Manual Override Project)2. The company's owner had no post-secondary education in science or engineering, none of its designers held an academic engineering degree or professional engineer (P.Eng.) designation, no P.Eng. was consulted on the experiments, and no employees with engineering training testified at the hearing82. The Court held that it was not provided with reliable evidence that the experimentation went beyond routine engineering, underscoring that technological uncertainty is measured against competent professionals in the field rather than untrained personnel82.
6.4 Modern Appellate and Trial Jurisprudence: Kam-Press Metal Products (2021 FCA 88), National R&D Inc. (2022 FCA 72), and Canafric Inc. (2023 TCC 108)

In National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (aff'g 2020 TCC 47), and Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88, the Federal Court of Appeal reaffirmed that the five-question test from Northwest Hydraulic remains the binding legal interpretation of subsection 248(1) of the ITA18. In National R&D, the FCA rejected the taxpayer's argument that the CRA's August 2021 SR&ED eligibility guidelines (which framed the analysis around the "Why" and "How" requirements) removed the requirement to follow the scientific method, holding that CRA administrative commentary is not binding on the courts18. The FCA also upheld the exclusion of the taxpayer's expert report, warning that expert witnesses owe an overriding duty of impartiality to the court, must not act as advocates or introduce unproven facts "through the back door," and cannot decide the ultimate legal question of whether work constitutes SR&ED79.

Finally, in Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 108, Chief Justice Rossiter of the Tax Court of Canada allowed all seven disputed SR&ED projects claimed by a frozen pie manufacturer for recipe development (reducing fat and salt, replacing ingredients, extending shelf-life, and reducing cooking time) across the 2013 to 2016 taxation years85. Rejecting the CRA Research and Technology Advisor's dismissive comment ("A pie is a pie, what is the big deal about it"), Chief Justice Rossiter cited National R&D (2022 FCA 72 at para 12) to hold that the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria must be applied in a context-sensitive, case-by-case manner suited to non-traditional shop-floor and food-manufacturing industries rather than through the narrow lens of traditional academic laboratory science89.
